1.thesis: A personal site built like a product: served in twenty languages, verified by a layered test plan, and with every decision written up in public.
1.heroAlt: The theabdullahfolio home page: the name in orange above a laptop on a lantern-lit stone path, ringed by navigation buttons, under a live GitHub status bar.

overview.body: theabdullahfolio is the portfolio you are reading. It is a Next.js site that doubles as its own case study: each page is a working sample of how I build software, from the first byte a visitor downloads to the notes that explain why it was built that way.

statement.title: The problem
statement.body: Most portfolios are brochures. They list what someone has made, but never show how it was made. This one had to be the evidence itself: as accountable as a product, as accessible as a public service, and open to anyone who wants to check the work.

arrive.title: Arrive
arrive.body: The home page paints its name and a ring of destinations first. Animation features arrive afterwards in their own chunk, so nothing a visitor needs waits for motion to download.
arrive.alt: The home page with its orbit of navigation buttons around the name.

language.title: Read in your language
language.body: Every page is served in twenty languages. Four of them read right to left, and the layout mirrors with them: margins, arrows, motion and typed input all follow the reader’s direction.
language.alt: The about page in Arabic, laid out right to left.

palette.title: Move by keyboard
palette.body: A command palette on every page reaches each route, project and section by typing. It also has an Ask panel that answers questions about the work and cites the page each answer came from.
palette.alt: The command palette open over the projects page, listing the site’s routes.

receipts.title: Check the receipts
receipts.body: The engineering notes are published as pages, and the uses page reads its figures from the build itself: the test counts, the dependency versions and the deployment pipeline.
receipts.alt: The uses page: the machine and the editor bench, each row confirmed by the owner.

about.alt: The about page: the most-used languages and GitHub statistics, read live from GitHub, beside the years-in-the-craft card.
about.caption: About: live counts from GitHub and the CV.

journey.alt: The journey page: a timeline of study and work.
journey.caption: Journey: the timeline, era by era.

projects.alt: The projects listing with category tabs.
projects.caption: Projects: filtered by category.

notes.alt: An engineering note rendered as a long-form page.
notes.caption: Notes: decisions, written up in public.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.body: Pages are rendered on the server and prerendered at build wherever they can be. Content and translations are files in the repository, and live figures come through a few small API routes. Each of those routes keeps its credentials on the server.

stack.title: Built with
stack.body: A mainstream stack kept deliberately small: one framework, one styling system, one translation library, and a handful of libraries that each do one job.

lazy-motion.title: Motion that is allowed to arrive late
lazy-motion.body: The animation engine left every first load. Elements describe their end state in props, so a page that never receives the motion chunk is still complete. Rejected: shipping the whole library up front.

languages.title: Twenty languages, four right to left
languages.body: Copy is translated by message, then validated for placeholders and plurals. Layout uses logical properties only. Rejected: an English site with a translate button.

testing.title: A test plan that is published
testing.body: Unit, property, mutation, component, API, end-to-end, accessibility, visual, performance and security layers, each written down with what it does not catch. Rejected: coverage as the goal.

restraint.title: Words before WebGL
restraint.body: This page used to be a 3D laptop on a tree stump. It now explains the work instead of staging it, and three.js has left the route. Rejected: a scene that hid the content and cost a GPU.
